memory-retrieval/testing-effect.claim: Retrieving studied material from memory (for example, writing down everything you can recall with the book closed) improves retention at a delay of days or more, compared with spending the same time restudying it.

memory-retrieval/retrieval-feedback.claim: Checking recall against the source right after retrieving it increases the retention benefit and corrects errors that would otherwise persist. Without feedback, errors produced during recall tend to be retained.
memory-retrieval/retrieval-feedback.construct: feedback in test-enhanced learning; self-scoring accuracy

memory-retrieval/hypercorrection.claim: Errors a person made with high confidence are more likely to be corrected on a later test, once feedback is seen, than errors made with low confidence.

memory-retrieval/pretesting.claim: Trying to answer questions about material before studying it, even when most answers are wrong, improves later retention of that material compared with studying it without a pretest.

memory-retrieval/retrieval-before-review.claim: Opening a study session by retrieving earlier material before restudying it improves learning from the restudy that follows, compared with restudying first.

memory-retrieval/distributed-practice.claim: Spreading the same amount of study or retrieval across sessions separated by days produces better long-term retention than massing it into one session.

memory-retrieval/spacing-gap-ratio.claim: For a fixed retention interval, the gap between sessions that maximises retention is a fraction of that interval, and that fraction shrinks as the interval grows. For a target of about one month, gaps of about 1, 3 and 7 days fall in or near the high-retention region.
memory-retrieval/spacing-gap-ratio.construct: the spacing lag × retention interval interaction (the "temporal ridgeline")
memory-retrieval/spacing-gap-ratio.suggested_rewording: For a fixed retention interval, the gap that maximises retention is a fraction of that interval (about 20–40% at one week, 5–10% at one year), so for a one-month target the best gaps are several days to about a week; gaps that are too short cost more than gaps that are too long. (A, adjacent)
memory-retrieval/spacing-gap-ratio.parameter_recommendation: revise to gaps of about a week for the ≈1-month target retention interval. The implied gap ratio is ≈15–25%, with the retention interval counted from the last session. At minimum, lengthen the 1-day first gap to 3 days or more: it sits below the interpolated optimum, and short gaps are the costly side of the ridgeline. Record the target interval and the ratio with the style. Read together with expanding-vs-uniform, this points to roughly equal gaps of about a week.

memory-retrieval/expanding-vs-uniform.claim: An expanding schedule of retrieval gaps (for example 1d → 3d → 7d) produces better long-term retention than a uniform schedule with the same total spacing.
memory-retrieval/expanding-vs-uniform.suggested_rewording: For long-term retention, delaying the first retrieval matters more than the shape of the schedule; once the first retrieval is delayed, expanding the gaps adds little over equal gaps, and equal gaps did better at a delay. (C, adjacent; B if Latimier et al. 2021 is read and agrees)
memory-retrieval/expanding-vs-uniform.parameter_recommendation: revise to uniform spacing. The uniform option is the better supported, and §8 says to pick the better-graded option. The Series schedule should use equal gaps, for example about 7d/7d/7d, not 1d/3d/7d. Under ruling 4 this does not move Series' grade.

memory-retrieval/successive-relearning.claim: Retrieving items to a criterion across several spaced sessions, and dropping or targeting items according to the previous session's failures, gives durable retention. Returns diminish after about three relearning sessions.
memory-retrieval/successive-relearning.suggested_rewording: Relearning items to a criterion across several spaced sessions gives durable retention, and each added session helps by a shrinking amount through at least five sessions; three is a sensible minimum, not the point where gains stop. (C, adjacent; B once Rawson et al. 2013 and the Higham et al. 2022 replication are read)
memory-retrieval/successive-relearning.parameter_recommendation: keep 3 sessions as a design choice, labelled a minimum, not the point of greatest return. Never print or document that returns diminish after three. Keep "each round targets the previous round's gaps", but revise it so that correctly recalled items stay in later rounds: targeting should add prompts for gaps, not drop what was recalled.

memory-retrieval/interleaving-confusable.claim: Interleaving practice across confusable categories or problem types improves later discrimination and problem solving compared with blocked practice. The benefit shrinks, or reverses, for dissimilar categories and for verbal or expository material.
memory-retrieval/interleaving-confusable.parameter_recommendation: keep, supported. Mix types within a round only when the categories are confusable, and never by default for word lists or expository notes.

memory-retrieval/self-explanation.claim: Prompting learners to explain to themselves why each step of given material follows improves understanding and transfer, compared with studying the same material without such prompts.
memory-retrieval/self-explanation.suggested_rewording: Prompting learners to explain to themselves why each step of given material follows improves their learning of that material, compared with studying it without prompts. (A, adjacent, pending a heterogeneity check on Bisra et al. 2018)

memory-retrieval/worked-example-fading.claim: For novices, studying worked examples whose final steps are progressively removed (completion problems) improves learning compared with unaided problem solving. The advantage shrinks or reverses as expertise grows.
memory-retrieval/worked-example-fading.construct: the worked-example effect with fading, and the expertise-reversal effect

memory-retrieval/elaborative-interrogati.claim: Prompting learners to answer "why is this true?" for stated facts improves recall of those facts compared with reading them.

memory-retrieval/explanatory-depth.claim: People overestimate how well they understand how things work. Attempting a step-by-step explanation lowers that self-rating, which exposes the gap.

memory-retrieval/explaining-to-learn.claim: Explaining material to an imagined novice in one's own words improves understanding and retention compared with restudying it.

memory-retrieval/generate-before-told.claim: Attempting an answer yourself before being given one improves later understanding and retention, compared with receiving the answer first.
memory-retrieval/generate-before-told.construct: the generation effect; productive failure (problem solving before instruction)

memory-retrieval/practice-specificity.claim: Practice transfers to a target skill to the extent that the practice's cues and required actions resemble the target's. A study method that exercises a different process from the one the test or task demands transfers poorly.
memory-retrieval/practice-specificity.construct: transfer-appropriate processing; identical elements; near vs far transfer
memory-retrieval/practice-specificity.suggested_rewording: Practice transfers best when it demands the same kind of retrieval or response as the target task, and transfer to a different skill is rare; what should match is the processing demanded, not the surface conditions, which are often better varied. (B, adjacent)

free-recall.helps: when studied material has to last days or weeks: writing out what you remember with the book closed, then checking it against the source in a second colour, beats rereading for the same time on a later test, by a small to moderate margin in this free-recall format, though not on a test minutes away
free-recall.backfires: when so little comes back that there is nothing to check, or when the check pass is skipped or scored loosely: errors recalled without correction tend to persist, and people marking their own recall credit wrong answers unless they check it idea by idea

free-recall/with-confidence.helps: when some recalled answers feel certain: errors made with high confidence are the ones most readily corrected once checked, and the dots show which corrections matter most
free-recall/with-confidence.backfires: when a correction is not revisited: a week later, corrected high-confidence errors were the likeliest to come back

free-recall/cued.helps: when used before first studying a text: attempting the prompts first, even with wrong answers, improves later memory for the prompted material, provided the answers are then studied
free-recall/cued.backfires: when the answers are never studied afterwards, or when the prompts narrow reading to the prompted parts, which studies of reading (though not of video) have reported

self-explain.helps: when working through stepwise material you are learning: prompts to explain why each step follows improve learning across a range of conditions, though evidence for transfer, for classroom use and for retention after a delay is thinner
self-explain.backfires: when the material already comes fully explained: given explanations crowded out learners' own and lowered learning, while making them feel they had learned more

self-explain/faded.helps: when the procedure is new to you: removing worked steps from the end helped near transfer more than pairing examples with problems, in a few studies
self-explain/faded.backfires: when you already know the procedure: techniques that help novices can lose their benefit, or hurt, for more experienced learners (expertise reversal)

self-explain/why.helps: when you already know something about the topic: answering "why is this true?" for facts is rated a moderately useful technique, on limited evidence
self-explain/why.backfires: when the topic is new to you, so the "why" answers have little to draw on

feynman.helps: when you feel you understand how something works: trying to explain the mechanism step by step reliably lowers people's rating of their own understanding, which shows where the gap is
feynman.backfires: when the page gets a list of reasons or opinions instead of a mechanism, which did not reduce the illusion, or when the exposed gap is taken for learning: in pre-registered replications, explaining changed people's ratings of their understanding but not their views

question-queue.helps: when a question can wait until the page has been worked: trying an answer yourself before being told improves later understanding on average, though deferring an AI's answer has not itself been tested
question-queue.backfires: when the parked question blocks the work on the page, or when the material is new and complex enough that working without guidance costs more than it teaches, as it did for young learners and for domain-general skills

series.helps: when material has to be remembered for weeks: recalling it across sessions days apart, and recalling before rereading, beats massing the same study into one sitting
series.backfires: when sessions bunch together or the first recall comes too soon after study, when word lists or notes from unrelated categories are mixed in one round, or when the schedule is dropped for cramming because massed study feels more effective

practice-audit.helps: when a study or practice method may not exercise what the real task demands: practice transfers best when it calls for the same kind of response as the target, and transfer to a different skill is rare; the four-question audit itself is untested craft
practice-audit.backfires: when "resemble the target" is read as copying its surface conditions: varying practice conditions often improves retention, and context effects fade when practice does not rely on the surroundings
